nodes.title: Keep every state change in one pure reducer

anchor.snippet: function pickerReducer(state: PickerState, action: PickerAction): PickerState {

nodes.why: Both versions send the same actions to the same function, so the port cannot drift: a key that moves the active option in the class moves it in React too, and the logic can be tested without a DOM.
nodes.alternative: Write the open and keyboard logic twice, once in the class methods and once in React handlers.
nodes.tradeoff: The reducer needs a small action vocabulary up front, but every behaviour then has one definition.

nodes.title: Return the same state when nothing changes
nodes.why: Callers compare the previous and next object: the class skips render() and onChange, and React skips a re-render. A click outside an already closed picker therefore costs nothing.
nodes.alternative: Always return a fresh object and let each caller diff the fields.
nodes.tradeoff: Identity checks are cheap and simple, but every branch has to remember to return the original object when it changes nothing.

nodes.title: Prevent the default only for keys the picker handles

anchor.snippet: function handlesKey(state: PickerState, key: string): boolean {

nodes.why: Arrow keys would scroll the page and Enter on an open list would also click the button and reopen it. Enter and Space on a closed trigger are left alone so the native button click opens the list.
nodes.alternative: Call preventDefault() for every keydown on the trigger.
nodes.tradeoff: Blocking every key breaks Tab and browser shortcuts; a named list keeps native behaviour where the picker has nothing to add.

nodes.title: Build the class DOM once and update it in place
nodes.why: render() only writes text and attributes onto nodes created in the constructor, so the focused trigger is never replaced and a click target stays inside the picker while the document listener checks it.
nodes.alternative: Rebuild the markup with innerHTML or replaceChildren on every state change.
nodes.tradeoff: In-place updates mean a little more code per attribute, but focus, listeners and click targets survive every update.

nodes.title: Write labels with textContent
nodes.why: Labels can come from users. textContent shows "My preset <draft>" literally, while innerHTML would create a draft element and open the door to injected markup.
nodes.alternative: Build an HTML string with the labels and assign it with innerHTML.
nodes.tradeoff: textContent needs one node per label, which the class creates anyway.

nodes.title: Handle every option with one delegated listener
nodes.why: One click listener on the list finds the option with closest() and reads its index from data-index, so options need no listeners of their own and there is less to remove in destroy().
nodes.alternative: Add a click listener to each li when it is created.
nodes.tradeoff: Delegation relies on the DOM structure and a data attribute, but it scales to long lists and keeps cleanup to one call.

nodes.title: Keep handlers as arrow-function fields
nodes.why: Arrow-function fields keep this bound to the instance and give addEventListener and removeEventListener the same function reference, which is what removal needs.
nodes.alternative: Pass this.method.bind(this) or an inline arrow function to addEventListener.
nodes.tradeoff: Fields allocate one function per instance, which is fine for a picker and avoids the silent no-op removal that new bound functions cause.

nodes.title: Remove every listener in destroy()
nodes.why: The document listener outlives the picker unless it is removed; the wrapper calls destroy() when React unmounts it, and the unmount check counts listeners left on document.
nodes.alternative: Rely on removing the root element to clean up.
nodes.tradeoff: Removing the root drops listeners on its own nodes, but not the one on document, which keeps the instance alive and keeps closing nothing.

nodes.title: Report a change only when the selection moves
nodes.why: send() compares the selected index before and after the reducer, so choosing the selected option again or moving the active option reports nothing.
nodes.alternative: Call onChange after every choose action.
nodes.tradeoff: The comparison is one line, and it keeps the callback meaningful for analytics or saving.

nodes.title: Port the state with useReducer and the same reducer
nodes.why: useReducer takes the exact function the class calls, so the port changes where state lives, not what it does. The lazy initializer computes the selected index once.
nodes.alternative: Rewrite the state as several useState calls inside the component.
nodes.tradeoff: The reducer keeps both versions aligned; separate useState calls would be shorter here but would duplicate the transitions.

nodes.title: Pair the document listener with an effect cleanup
nodes.why: The effect plays the role of the constructor and destroy() pair: it adds the listener after mount and removes it on unmount. dispatch is stable, so the listener never reads stale state.
nodes.alternative: Add the listener during render or in an effect without a cleanup.
nodes.tradeoff: An effect runs after paint, which is fine for outside clicks; without the cleanup every unmount would leak a listener.

nodes.title: Keep onChange in event handlers
nodes.why: Running the same reducer on the current state tells the handler whether the selection will change before it dispatches. The reducer stays pure and no effect fires onChange on mount.
nodes.alternative: Watch selectedIndex in a useEffect and call onChange there.
nodes.tradeoff: Computing the next state twice is cheap; an effect would report a change nobody made on the first render.

nodes.title: Return focus to the trigger after a mouse choice
nodes.why: Keyboard users can keep working after picking with the mouse, and screen readers announce the new value on the focused combobox.
nodes.alternative: Leave focus wherever the click left it.
nodes.tradeoff: One focus call in the handler; the class does the same with this.trigger.focus().

nodes.title: Keep the list mounted and toggle hidden
nodes.why: aria-controls always points at a real element and the React markup matches the class markup, so the same checks apply to both versions.
nodes.alternative: Render the list only while it is open.
nodes.tradeoff: A hidden list keeps its nodes in the DOM, which is negligible for four options.
